prose.summary: An SEO specialist decides what a site needs to say, and how it needs to be built, so that search engines and the people using them find it on purpose rather than by accident. The job sits closer to data analysis than people expect: you spend more time in Search Console pulling apart a ranking drop than you spend writing anything. The role next to it, content strategist, decides what gets said. SEO decides whether anyone ever sees it.
prose.day_to_day: Most weeks start with a look at the previous week's traffic and ranking movement, usually in Semrush or Google Analytics, checking for anything that dropped hard enough to need an explanation before a client or a boss asks for one. From there the work splits between technical audits (crawl errors, page speed, rendering issues that keep pages out of the index) and content work: briefs, keyword clusters, edits to pages that are close to ranking but not quite there. There's usually one stretch of the week that's pure heads-down analysis and one or two meetings where you walk a stakeholder through why a page tanked or a competitor jumped three spots. The moment people look forward to is watching a page you rewrote six weeks ago finally clear onto page one, because SEO has enough lag that you rarely get to celebrate anything the same week you did it. Roughly a third of the week involves other people; the rest is solo, in tabs, cross-referencing data that doesn't agree with itself. By Friday you've usually got a short list of pages to watch and a longer list of technical fixes waiting on a developer.
prose.work_environment: This is a desk job end to end, and the 70 percent remote share reflects that: nothing about SEO requires being in a specific building, since the work is reading dashboards, writing briefs, and talking to developers who are often remote themselves. The bad weeks come from algorithm updates, when Google changes its ranking approach overnight and every account you manage needs re-diagnosing at once, or from reporting season, when every client wants a quarterly review on the same week. There's no on-call in the emergency sense, but a sudden 40 percent traffic drop on a client's biggest revenue page has the same urgency without the phone ringing at 2am. Hours are steady outside of those spikes, generally a standard week with meetings clustered on two or three days.
prose.getting_in: The degree picture is mixed: most postings list a bachelor's as required, a smaller share prefer one, and a few waive it outright for candidates who can show ranking results, which in practice means a portfolio of sites you've moved up in search or a case study from a previous job. The median experience asked for is two years, and that's the step where people stall, because the entry-level SEO postings are thin and most roles want someone who has already fixed a site, not someone who has only read about fixing one. The fastest real path is landing a marketing generalist or content role first, picking up SEO as one of your duties, and building a track record over twelve to eighteen months before applying for the title directly. Certifications in Semrush or Google Analytics help get past applicant tracking systems but nobody hires on the certificate alone; they hire on the traffic graph you can show them.
prose.ladder: Early on you own individual pages or a small content section: you're told what to improve and you improve it. The step up is owning a whole site's architecture and the roadmap behind it, which means defending priorities to a marketing manager rather than just executing a brief. Past that the ladder forks: one path goes into managing a team of specialists and freelancers across multiple client accounts, the other stays hands-on but shifts toward technical SEO, working directly with engineering on rendering and site structure, which is a specialist track more than a management one. Most people who are going to fork do it somewhere between year three and year five, once they've run at least one site through a full year of seasonal cycles.
prose.suits: People who like this job tend to be the sort who find a ranking-drop mystery satisfying to solve, the kind who'll cross-reference three data sources at 6pm because they want to know why, not because anyone asked them to stay late. It rewards someone comfortable holding two skill sets at once, writing and analysis, without needing to be the best in the room at either. People who leave are usually the ones who wanted to write for a living and got frustrated that half their week is spreadsheets, or the ones who wanted fast feedback and couldn't get used to changes taking six to twelve weeks to show up in the numbers. If you want to see the result of your work today, this isn't that job.
prose.misconceptions: Outsiders think SEO is mostly keyword stuffing or tricking an algorithm, when the actual work in 2024 postings leans heavily on data analysis and technical fixes (rendering, crawl budgets, site speed) that have nothing to do with sneaky tricks. There's also a belief that SEO is dying because of AI search summaries; the postings say otherwise so far, with 41 percent already asking for LLM-related skills, meaning the job is absorbing AI as another surface to optimize for rather than being replaced by it.
prose.who_qualifies: Marketing managers carry over the strongest, since they've already run campaigns and read the same analytics dashboards, just without the search-specific depth. Content strategists bring the writing and editorial judgment but usually need to build up the technical and data side. Copywriters and social media managers transfer some of the audience instinct but tend to be furthest from the technical requirements, and usually need real time with Search Console and a crawler tool like Screaming Frog before they're job-ready.
prose.what_the_numbers_miss: The postings can't show you what it feels like to watch six months of work get erased by a single algorithm update that has nothing to do with your work quality. They also can't capture how much of the job is translating technical findings into language a non-technical stakeholder will act on, which is its own skill entirely separate from the SEO itself.

steps.do: Learn SEO fundamentals and one analytics platform
steps.how: Work through Google's own Search Central documentation and get comfortable in Google Analytics and Search Console using a real site, even a personal blog. This takes 4 to 8 weeks of steady evening study. You're done when you can explain why a specific page isn't ranking, using actual data, not a guess.

steps.do: Run an SEO project on a real site
steps.how: Pick a site with existing traffic, ideally your own or a small business willing to let you experiment, and take it through a full audit and fix cycle: technical issues, content gaps, internal linking. Give it 8 to 12 weeks to show movement, since rankings lag behind changes. Done means you have a before-and-after traffic graph you didn't have to explain away.

steps.do: Get functional in Semrush or Ahrefs
steps.how: Semrush shows up in 63 percent of postings, so fluency in one major keyword and competitor research tool is close to a requirement. Spend 2 to 3 weeks running keyword gap analyses and competitor audits until you can pull a report without a tutorial open in another tab.

steps.do: Land a generalist role with SEO duties
steps.how: Apply for marketing coordinator or content marketing roles that list SEO as one responsibility among several, since pure entry-level SEO titles are rare. Plan on 12 to 18 months in that seat, using it to accumulate the two years of hands-on experience most SEO-titled postings ask for.

steps.do: Build a portfolio of ranking outcomes
steps.how: Collect two or three case studies with specific before-and-after numbers (traffic, ranking position, conversion lift) from your generalist role or freelance work. This is what gets you past the experience gate in job applications, more than any certificate, and it's the thing hiring managers ask to see in an interview.

prose.tools: Semrush and Google Analytics are the two real gatekeepers, showing up in well over half of postings, and you won't get past a screening call without working knowledge of at least one. Data analysis skills generally (57 percent of postings) matter as much as any single tool, since the job is about reading numbers correctly. HTML/CSS and JavaScript show up in over a quarter of postings, mostly for technical SEO roles that need to read and sometimes edit code directly. LLM-related skills are newer (41 percent) and growing, reflecting how much SEO work now involves optimizing for AI-generated search summaries alongside traditional rankings.

industries.name: SaaS and B2B software
industries.note: Long sales cycles mean SEO here is about ranking for specific technical terms a buyer searches months before purchasing; content is dense and often written with an engineer or product manager as co-author.

industries.name: E-commerce
industries.note: Faster feedback loops than most industries, since a ranking change shows up in revenue within weeks, but the technical side (site speed, product page templates at scale) gets heavier.

industries.name: Digital marketing agencies
industries.note: You run multiple client accounts at once, which means more reporting and more context-switching, but you see a wider range of industries and problems than staying in-house.

industries.name: Media and publishing
industries.note: Volume-driven work, often dozens of articles a week, where the SEO job is closer to editorial strategy at scale than to any single technical fix.

specializations.name: Technical SEO
specializations.why: Requires real comfort with rendering, JavaScript, and site architecture, which fewer generalists have; postings that need it tend to pay toward the upper end of the range and the skill doesn't commoditize as fast as content-side SEO.

specializations.name: SEO for AI search and LLM visibility
specializations.why: With 41 percent of postings already naming LLM skills, this is the fastest-moving part of the field: figuring out how to get cited or summarized correctly by AI search products, which is a different discipline from ranking in a traditional results list.

specializations.name: International or multilingual SEO
specializations.why: Companies hiring across the US, Germany, UK, and Hungary need specialists who can handle hreflang tags, regional keyword differences, and localized content strategy, and there are fewer people who do this well than who do single-market SEO.

pros: Watching a page you rewrote climb from page three to the top of page one gives you a specific, checkable win that most marketing work never provides.
The mix of writing and data analysis means no two days look quite the same, and you're rarely stuck doing only one kind of task for a full week.
Remote work is close to the default here (70 percent of postings), so you can build a career without being tied to a specific city.
The skill compounds: once you understand how search engines evaluate a site, that knowledge holds even as tools and algorithms change around it.
cons: Results lag weeks or months behind the work, so you often can't tell if something worked until long after you've moved on to the next task.
Algorithm updates can erase months of gains overnight for reasons Google doesn't fully explain, and you're the one who has to explain it to whoever's asking.
A meaningful share of the job is proving your value to people who don't understand what you did, which means a lot of translating technical findings into slides.
The entry-level path is thin: most postings want two years of experience already, so the first job is harder to land than the fifth.

faq.q: how long does it take to become an seo specialist
faq.a: Plan on roughly a year to eighteen months if you start from a related marketing role, since most postings ask for around two years of hands-on experience and there aren't many entry-level SEO-titled jobs to start in directly. The fastest route is picking up SEO duties inside a broader marketing or content job first, then applying for the specialist title once you have a portfolio of ranking results to show.

faq.q: do you need a degree to be an seo specialist
faq.a: Most postings list a bachelor's as required, but a real minority waive it entirely if you can show results: sites you've ranked, traffic graphs, case studies. A marketing, communications, or even English degree is common among people already in the role, but the degree matters far less than a track record once you're past the first application screen.

faq.q: is seo a good career right now with ai search taking over
faq.a: The postings suggest it's holding up rather than shrinking, with 41 percent already asking for LLM-related skills, meaning employers are treating AI search as a new surface to optimize for, not a replacement for the role. It does mean the job is shifting: less pure keyword work, more understanding of how AI systems summarize and cite content.

Yes, and it's closer to the norm than the exception: 70 percent of current postings are remote. The work is dashboards, writing, and calls, none of which require a physical location, which is also why hiring is spread across multiple countries rather than concentrated in one office hub.

faq.q: seo specialist vs content strategist, what's the difference
faq.a: A content strategist decides what a site should say and to whom; an SEO specialist decides whether anyone will ever find it, which means more time in analytics tools and technical audits and less time drafting the actual copy. The two roles overlap enough (a 50 percent skill match between them) that people move between them, but SEO leans data-and-technical where content strategy leans editorial.
